lines.text: You know what each tier of the machine costs. An index decides how many of those costs a lookup has to pay.
There are two great families, and the whole topic is the question of where each one makes you pay.
One pays when it writes. The other pays when it reads.
The first family keeps data sorted, in place, in a tree. Look at the shape: every node is exactly one page.
The leaves hold the rows. The nodes above hold only signposts, telling a search which child to take.
The number that matters is how many signposts fit in a page. Page size divided by the size of one entry. That is the fan-out.
Hold on to it. Everything about this tree's speed comes from that one number being large.

tolerated.line: The leaves hold the rows. The nodes above hold only signposts, telling a search which child to take.

lines.text: A hundred million keys, a fan-out of a few hundred.
Do not count nodes. Ask how many times you can divide a hundred million by a few hundred before one is left.
How many levels is that?
Three or four.
The height is a logarithm of the key count, in the base of the fan-out. A large base makes a logarithm small.
Twenty or ten levels would be right for a binary tree, where the base is two. The tree is short because it is wide, and key size changes the answer only through the fan-out.

tolerated.line: The height is a logarithm of the key count, in the base of the fan-out. A large base makes a logarithm small.

lines.text: So a point lookup walks one path from root to leaf. Three or four pages.
But look at which pages. The root is one page. The level below it is a few megabytes at most.
Those pages are touched by every lookup, so after a handful of queries they sit in memory for good.
That is the real cost: about one read from the drive, at the leaf. And a range scan descends once, then walks sideways along linked leaves.
The second family refuses to write in place. Watch what a write does here: it only ever appends.
It goes into a small sorted table in memory. When that fills, the table is frozen and flushed in one long sequential sweep. That output is a sorted run.
Notice what is missing. No page to hunt for, no seek, no read before the write.
That is why ingestion is so cheap. The structure was designed so the disk only ever sees sequential writes.

tolerated.line: Notice what is missing. No page to hunt for, no seek, no read before the write.
That is why ingestion is so cheap. The structure was designed so the disk only ever sees sequential writes.

lines.text: But there is a price. Runs are never modified, so they pile up, and a reader has to look in more of them.
So a background job merges several runs into fewer, larger ones. That is compaction, and it is the same merge of sorted inputs you will meet in external sorting.
The catch is on the right of the picture. Each level is about ten times the one above, and a byte is rewritten every time it moves down.
So the cheap writes were not free. The cost moved to the background, where the disk does the rewriting.

tolerated.line: So the cheap writes were not free. The cost moved to the background, where the disk does the rewriting.
So the cheap writes were not free. The cost moved to the background, where the disk does the rewriting.

lines.text: Now weigh the two, on three costs: reading, writing, and space.
The in-place tree reads beautifully, one cached path. But a tiny change rewrites a whole page, and the log writes it again.
The append-only tree writes beautifully. But a read may touch several runs, and compaction rewrites data many times over.
Read the two numbers at the bottom: leveled write amplification near thirty three, space near one point one four. Those are RocksDB's own worked example, not a law.

lines.text: Researchers gave this trade a name. Reads, updates, memory.
The conjecture says you can push at most two of them down, and the third pays.
Our two families sit at opposite corners of that triangle. The in-place tree buys cheap reads. The append-only tree buys cheap writes.
So no design wins everywhere. The question is always which cost your workload can afford.

tolerated.line: Our two families sit at opposite corners of that triangle. The in-place tree buys cheap reads. The append-only tree buys cheap writes.

lines.text: An obvious objection: if a read must check many runs, surely it is slow.
That is what the membership sketch is for. Before opening a run, you ask whether the key could possibly be inside.
Most of the time the answer is no, so a point read touches about one run. The default spends ten bits per key for roughly a one percent mistake rate.
Now notice what the sketch cannot do. It answers exact keys only. A range scan has nothing to ask it, so it still merges every overlapping run.

tolerated.line: An obvious objection: if a read must check many runs, surely it is slow.

lines.text: Make it concrete with the shop. You look up one order by its id, over and over. Reads dominate.
Which family do you reach for?
The in-place tree.
A short descent through pages that are already cached, then a tidy walk along the leaves if you need neighbours.
The append-only tree would work, but you would be paying for run checks on every read to gain a write speed you are not using. That is why operational databases default to the tree.

tolerated.line: A short descent through pages that are already cached, then a tidy walk along the leaves if you need neighbours.

lines.text: Now the opposite extreme. A terabyte of order events arriving as a stream, mostly appends.
Which family wants that workload?
The append-only tree.
It takes the stream at memory speed and leaves the sorting to background compaction, so the write path never seeks.
The in-place tree would rewrite a page for each small change, which turns a stream into a storm of random writes. You pay for it in reads and disk work later, but the ingest never stalls.

tolerated.line: It takes the stream at memory speed and leaves the sorting to background compaction, so the write path never seeks.

lines.text: One sentence decides it. The in-place tree trades write cost for read cost. The append-only tree trades read and space cost for write cost.
So do not ask which is better. Ask where your hot path is, and choose the structure whose cheap side is that path.
Next: what a lookup really costs when the index finds thousands of rows, counted in block transfers.
